Latent class growth analysis with the latents R package

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland
Source: vignettes/articles/trajectory-classes.Rmd
trajectory-classes.Rmd

Latent class growth analysis (LCGA), also known as group-based trajectory modelling, is a person-centred approach used to identify distinct subgroups of individuals who exhibit different patterns of change over time. When the same individuals are measured repeatedly, LCGA assumes that the population consists of a finite number of latent classes, each characterized by a specific developmental trajectory. These trajectories describe how the outcome of interest changes over time within each subgroup. Individuals are assigned to latent classes according to their posterior probabilities of membership, which indicate the extent to which their observed measurement patterns correspond to each estimated trajectory (Nagin, 2005).

Similar to latent profile analysis, LCGA focuses on identifying meaningful subgroups within a population, but rather than distinguishing individuals according to their patterns of responses at a particular point in time, it differentiates them according to their longitudinal patterns of development (Scrucca et al., 2024; Saqr et al., 2024). A defining feature of LCGA is the assumption that individuals within the same class share an identical underlying growth trajectory. Accordingly, within-class variation in individual growth parameters is constrained to zero, and deviations from the estimated trajectory are attributed to random measurement error. This assumption distinguishes LCGA from growth mixture modelling, which allows individuals within the same class to vary in their growth parameters and, consequently, in their individual developmental trajectories.

LCGA is a special case of mixture regression (see the mixture regression article). Time is the predictor, and the class is shared by all measurements of a person rather than assigned to each measurement separately. In latents it is therefore fitted with mixture_regression(), with time on the right of the formula and class_level = "group"; adding random effects through random turns the same call into a growth mixture model.

The assumption of identical trajectories within a class is both the strength and the limitation of the model:

  • Strength. The model is simple, fast to estimate and, as a mixture regression, accommodates every outcome family of mixture_regression(): continuous scores, binary outcomes, counts and ordered ratings.
  • Limitation. Individuals of the same kind rarely follow one trajectory exactly. When they vary around it, the model can represent that variation only by adding classes, and it therefore tends to identify more classes than there are kinds of individuals (Bauer & Curran, 2003). The growth mixture model adds random effects for that variation; it is the subject of the growth mixture article.

Fitting both models and comparing them with compare_models(), as the growth mixture article does, is therefore advisable.

Role Argument Here
Outcome, measured repeatedly left of ~ score
Time (any shape) right of ~ wave, wave + I(wave^2)
Person id, with class_level = "group" student
Kind of outcome family "gaussian", "binomial", "poisson", "negative_binomial", "ordinal"
What predicts the class membership "motivation"

The data

growth_scores is simulated so the answer is known: 300 students tested on up to seven waves, of three kinds (improving, stable, declining), each student varying a little around their kind’s trajectory, with motivation predicting the kind. Missed tests (about 12%) need no imputation.

library(latents)
head(growth_scores)
#>   student wave score motivation trajectory
#> 1       1    0  60.2      -0.72  declining
#> 2       1    2  49.7      -0.72  declining
#> 3       1    3  49.2      -0.72  declining
#> 4       1    4  44.9      -0.72  declining
#> 5       1    5  44.4      -0.72  declining
#> 6       1    6  41.5      -0.72  declining

Fitting and choosing the number of classes

Persons are the classified units, so id names them and class_level = "group" keeps all of a person’s measurements in one class.

enumerate_regressions(score ~ wave, growth_scores, n_classes = 1:5,
                      id = "student", class_level = "group",
                      n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
#> Mixture regression class enumeration
#> 
#>  n_classes n_group_classes log_likelihood n_parameters   bic   icl entropy smallest_share
#>          1               1          -6629            3 13276 13276      NA         1.0000
#>          2               1          -6080            7 12199 12210  0.9725         0.3263
#>          3               1          -5890           11 11842 11897  0.9156         0.3178
#>          4               1          -5778           15 11641 11689  0.9419         0.1376
#>          5               1          -5658           19 11425 11487  0.9359         0.1248
#>  converged best_bic
#>       TRUE    FALSE
#>       TRUE    FALSE
#>       TRUE    FALSE
#>       TRUE    FALSE
#>       TRUE     TRUE
#> 
#> One model: get_results(x, "model", n_classes = ).

The BIC keeps falling up to five classes (from 13,276 with one class to 11,425 with five), although only three kinds of student generated the data: the students’ own spread around their kind’s trajectory is absorbed by additional classes. With these data the growth mixture model, which models that spread, picks three. Here, to keep the three kinds, the three-class model is read:

fit <- mixture_regression(score ~ wave, growth_scores, n_classes = 3,
                          id = "student", class_level = "group",
                          membership = "motivation", n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
fit
#> Mixture of gaussian regressions: 3 classes (one class per `student`)
#> score ~ wave
#> 1844 rows in 300 groups | log likelihood -5848.9651 | BIC 11772.08 | entropy 0.917
#> Converged: TRUE | iterations: 22 | best likelihood reached by 6 of 6 completed starts (6 run)
#> 
#> Classes
#> 
#> Class    Share  Expected  Groups assigned  Avg. posterior  Residual SD
#> -------  -----  --------  ---------------  --------------  -----------
#> Class 1  0.345    103.43              104           0.945         5.16
#> Class 2  0.336    100.81              101           0.989         5.16
#> Class 3  0.319     95.76               95           0.949         4.71
#> 
#> Regression coefficients (95% CI)
#> 
#> Class    Term       Estimate          95% CI      p
#> -------  ---------  --------  --------------  -----
#> Class 1  Intercept     61.00  [60.00, 62.01]  <.001
#> Class 1  wave           1.05  [ 0.80,  1.31]  <.001
#> Class 2  Intercept     57.87  [57.12, 58.63]  <.001
#> Class 2  wave          -2.35  [-2.56, -2.14]  <.001
#> Class 3  Intercept     47.56  [46.60, 48.52]  <.001
#> Class 3  wave           3.37  [ 3.14,  3.61]  <.001
#> 
#> Every table: get_results(x, what = ), e.g. "classes", "membership", "fit", "assignments".

Every table is a data frame from get_results():

get_results(fit, "classes")
#> Classes
#> 
#> Class    Share  Expected  Groups assigned  Avg. posterior  Residual SD
#> -------  -----  --------  ---------------  --------------  -----------
#> Class 1  0.345    103.43              104           0.945         5.16
#> Class 2  0.336    100.81              101           0.989         5.16
#> Class 3  0.319     95.76               95           0.949         4.71
get_results(fit, "membership")
#> Class membership (log odds, 95% CI)
#> 
#> Class    Term        Estimate          95% CI      p  Odds ratio
#> -------  ----------  --------  --------------  -----  ----------
#> Class 2  Intercept      -0.28  [-0.62,  0.06]   .109            
#> Class 2  motivation     -1.01  [-1.39, -0.62]  <.001        0.36
#> Class 3  Intercept      -0.30  [-0.69,  0.09]   .127            
#> Class 3  motivation      0.62  [ 0.26,  0.99]  <.001        1.87
get_results(fit, "recovery", data = growth_scores, truth = "trajectory")
#> Recovery of a known classification
#> 
#> Assigned  trajectory  Groups  Share of assigned
#> --------  ----------  ------  -----------------
#> Class 1   improving       26              0.250
#> Class 2   improving        1              0.010
#> Class 3   improving       88              0.926
#> Class 1   stable          77              0.740
#> Class 2   stable           4              0.040
#> Class 3   stable           7              0.074
#> Class 1   declining        1              0.010
#> Class 2   declining       96              0.950
#> Class 3   declining        0              0.000

The three classes are an improving trajectory (class 3, 31.9% of the students, gaining 3.37 points per wave from 47.56), a declining trajectory (class 2, 33.6%, losing 2.35 points per wave from 57.87) and a stable trajectory (class 1, 34.5%, gaining 1.05 points per wave from 61.00). Higher motivation lowers the odds of the declining class relative to the stable one (odds ratio 0.36) and raises the odds of the improving class (odds ratio 1.87). Of the students assigned to the improving and declining classes, 92.6% and 95.0% were generated with those trajectories, whereas a quarter of the stable class (26 of 104 students) are improving students, whose spread around their trajectory the model does not represent.

Seeing the classes

Every view of a trajectory fit is one plot() call. Each class’s trajectory with its confidence band, the observed class means, and a sample of students’ observed trajectories as thin lines (a band for the spread of students around their class needs random effects, so it appears only in the growth mixture model):

plot(fit)

The same with one panel per class:

plot(fit, facet = TRUE)

Individual students, chosen across each class’s range of classification certainty: their observations and their class trajectory.

plot(fit, what = "individuals")

The coefficients with their intervals and p-values:

plot(fit, what = "coefficients")

How confidently each student is classified, one bar per student:

plot(fit, what = "classification")

Curved trajectories

Any formula works. A quadratic lets each class bend; compare it with the straight model fitted the same way (without membership):

straight <- mixture_regression(score ~ wave, growth_scores, n_classes = 3,
                               id = "student", class_level = "group",
                               n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
curved <- mixture_regression(score ~ wave + I(wave^2), growth_scores,
                             n_classes = 3, id = "student", class_level = "group",
                             n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
compare_models(straight = straight, curved = curved)
#> Model comparison
#> 
#> Model     Classes  Random   k    LogLik       BIC   ΔBIC  Weight  Entropy
#> --------  -------  ------  --  --------  --------  -----  ------  -------
#> straight        3  none    11  -5889.55  11841.85   0.00   1.000     0.92
#> curved          3  none    14  -5888.78  11857.41  15.56   0.000     0.92

These trajectories were generated as straight lines, and the BIC of the curved model is 15.6 points higher: the additional curvature is not supported.

plot(curved)

Outcomes that are not scores

For outcomes that are not continuous scores, latent class growth analysis is the available model: random effects for a binary, count or ordered outcome require numerical integration, which the growth mixture model in latents does not perform. An alternative for trajectories of categorical states is to identify the state of each person at each occasion and model the resulting sequences of states (López-Pernas & Saqr, 2023, 2024).

Pass or fail. Whether each test reached 60 points, with a logistic trajectory per class:

passing <- transform(growth_scores, passed = as.integer(score >= 60))
pass_fit <- mixture_regression(passed ~ wave, passing, n_classes = 3,
                               family = "binomial", id = "student",
                               class_level = "group", n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
get_results(pass_fit, "coefficients")
#> Regression coefficients (95% CI)
#> 
#> Class    Term       Estimate          95% CI      p  Odds ratio
#> -------  ---------  --------  --------------  -----  ----------
#> Class 1  Intercept     -0.74  [-1.14, -0.35]  <.001            
#> Class 1  wave          -0.75  [-1.07, -0.43]  <.001        0.47
#> Class 2  Intercept     -3.85  [-4.80, -2.91]  <.001            
#> Class 2  wave           1.14  [ 0.90,  1.39]  <.001        3.13
#> Class 3  Intercept      1.28  [ 0.40,  2.17]   .004            
#> Class 3  wave           0.42  [ 0.13,  0.71]   .005        1.52

Each class’s probability of passing over the waves, and the coefficients:

plot(pass_fit)

plot(pass_fit, what = "coefficients")

Ordered bands. The score in four ordered bands, with a cumulative-logit (proportional odds) trajectory per class (McCullagh, 1980): each class has its own thresholds between the bands and its own slope over the waves.

banded <- transform(growth_scores,
                    band = cut(score, c(-Inf, 52, 58, 64, Inf),
                               labels = c("low", "middle", "high", "top"),
                               ordered_result = TRUE))
band_fit <- mixture_regression(band ~ wave, banded, n_classes = 3,
                               family = "ordinal", id = "student",
                               class_level = "group", n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
get_results(band_fit, "coefficients")
#> Regression coefficients (95% CI)
#> 
#> Class    Term                   Estimate             95% CI      p  Odds ratio
#> -------  ---------------------  --------  -----------------  -----  ----------
#> Class 1  Threshold low|middle      1.107  [  0.663,  1.550]  <.001            
#> Class 1  Threshold middle|high     3.396  [  2.781,  4.010]  <.001            
#> Class 1  Threshold high|top        5.848  [  5.079,  6.617]  <.001            
#> Class 1  wave                      1.168  [  1.012,  1.323]  <.001        3.21
#> Class 2  Threshold low|middle     -2.115  [ -2.484, -1.745]  <.001            
#> Class 2  Threshold middle|high     0.100  [ -0.205,  0.404]   .520            
#> Class 2  Threshold high|top        2.913  [  2.195,  3.630]  <.001            
#> Class 2  wave                     -0.822  [ -0.951, -0.692]  <.001        0.44
#> Class 3  Threshold low|middle     -6.246  [-13.827,  1.335]   .106            
#> Class 3  Threshold middle|high    -1.538  [ -2.106, -0.971]  <.001            
#> Class 3  Threshold high|top        0.802  [  0.403,  1.202]  <.001            
#> Class 3  wave                      0.241  [  0.137,  0.346]  <.001        1.27

The plot shows each class’s expected band (1 = low to 4 = top), and the students’ own bands over the waves:

plot(band_fit)

plot(band_fit, what = "individuals")

Counts work the same way with family = "poisson", or family = "negative_binomial" when the counts are more spread out than a Poisson allows.

Distal outcomes

three_step() compares the classes on a variable measured once per person, using the bias-corrected three-step method (Vermunt, 2010; Bakk & Vermunt, 2016), which accounts for persons being classified with error. The trajectory model must be fitted without membership for this correction:

three_step(straight, data = growth_scores, outcome = "motivation",
           contrast = "pairs")
#> Distal outcome: class differences (bch, 95% CI)
#> 
#> Class  vs  Difference        95% CI      p  p (BH)
#> -----  --  ----------  ------------  -----  ------
#>     2   1        0.71  [0.46, 0.96]  <.001   <.001
#>     3   1        1.22  [0.96, 1.48]  <.001   <.001
#>     3   2        0.51  [0.24, 0.79]  <.001   <.001

All three pairs of classes differ in motivation (Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values below .001).

Choices and warnings

  • Latent class growth analysis and growth mixture models. When persons of the same kind vary around their trajectory, as they almost always do for scores, the growth mixture model is fitted as well and the two are compared with compare_models(); the growth mixture model is preferred when it fits better. Use latent class growth analysis for non-Gaussian outcomes, for a first look, and when within-class variation is not plausible.
  • Number of classes. Read the BIC with the over-extraction above in mind; the bootstrap likelihood-ratio test (enumerate_regressions(bootstrap =)) simulates from the same model without random effects. It can also favour extra classes that absorb omitted within-class variation. Compare the random-effects model as well; the bootstrap does not repair misspecification of its null model.
  • Starts. Several starts are used (n_starts), and the best likelihood should be reached more than once (the fit reports how many times).
